Algorithms and performance

When a correct program is still not good enough

Computing Bootcamp | Wednesday 21 October 2026

Stanislav (Stanley) Modrak
Draft MQB adaptation for contributor review

00:00–00:30. This session follows Tuesday’s debugging and profiling work. Students should already have seen that a working program can contain a slow part. Today asks a different question: how will the work grow when the input grows? The deck is a draft adaptation of Stanislav Modrak’s original lecture, itself adapted from teaching by Robert Sedgewick and Kevin Wayne.

Today’s question

Suppose a program works correctly for 1,000 observations.

Will it still be useful for 10,000—or one million?

We will combine two kinds of evidence:

  1. measurements from running programs; and
  2. a mathematical model of how their work grows.

00:30–02:00. Begin from a practical scientific decision. A successful run on a small example establishes neither correctness for every input nor useful performance at scale. Emphasise that measurements and models answer related but different questions.

Where this fits in the MQB workflow

Plan → implement → test → profile → analyse → improve → explain → rerun

  • Testing asks whether observed behaviour agrees with an independently expected result.
  • Profiling asks where a particular run spent its time.
  • Algorithm analysis asks how the required work changes with input size.

Correctness comes first. A fast wrong answer is still wrong—just sooner.

02:00–04:00. Connect directly to Monday and Tuesday. Do not present algorithm analysis as a replacement for testing or profiling. An optimisation must retain the program’s specified behaviour, and the comparison therefore needs common correctness checks.

Why study algorithms and data structures?

  • To solve problems that would otherwise be impractical
  • To predict whether a method will scale
  • To compare possible solutions before investing heavily in one
  • To understand the trade-offs between time, memory and clarity
  • To become a more thoughtful programmer

04:00–06:30. The original lecture motivates algorithms through scientific, intellectual and commercial impact. Retain that breadth, but bring the focus back to research: a better algorithm can make a previously impossible analysis possible. The image is an extracted original asset; attribution and reuse need confirmation during review.

Two ideas we need

Algorithm: a precise sequence of steps for solving a specified problem.

Data structure: a way of organising data so that useful operations can be carried out.

The same problem may have several correct algorithms. Their choice of data structure can change how much work they require.

06:30–09:00. Students have already used lists, dictionaries, sets and data frames. Make the connection explicit: these are not interchangeable containers. Their supported operations and costs shape possible algorithms.

A long history, not a new fashion

Long before electronic computers, people were already asking:

  • Which operations must be performed?
  • How many times must each operation be repeated?
  • Can the procedure be reorganised?

09:00–11:00. This retains the historical motivation from the original deck without relying on its exact machine-operation quotation. The extracted image is retained with the other source assets pending provenance review.

The practical questions

  1. Will the program solve a realistically large input in useful time?
  2. If not, what feature of the algorithm makes the work grow?
  3. Can we reduce that work without changing the answer?

11:00–13:00. The original lecture identifies performance bugs as the primary practical reason for analysis. Add the memory question now, rather than leaving it disconnected at the end.

Algorithms can change what science is feasible

  • Genome assembly became tractable through graph-based representations and algorithms that avoid comparing every possible reconstruction.
  • Ecological null models and simulations can often reuse quantities that have not changed instead of recalculating the entire state.

The important claim is not one universal complexity for either field. It is that reformulating the computation can remove enormous amounts of repeated work.

13:00–16:00. The source deck gives simplified linear-versus-quadratic examples for genome and community assembly. Those are useful motivations but too broad as general complexity claims. Keep the scientific examples while stating the mechanism modestly. Ask Stanislav to supply a precise reference if a numerical complexity claim is restored.

Develop the evidence in the right order

Problem → algorithm → implementation → measurement → model

16:00–18:30. An implementation mixes the algorithm with language, libraries, hardware and operating-system effects. We need it for experiments, but we should not mistake its measured time for a universal property of the algorithm.

Worked example: 3-SUM

Given a collection of distinct integers, how many triples sum to exactly zero?

For 30, -40, -20, -10, 40, 0, 10, 5, the expected answer is 4.

18:30–21:00. Establish the input assumptions and expected result before code. The original example says the integers are distinct; retain that condition because it matters when deciding what counts as a different triple.

A transparent brute-force algorithm

def count_three_sum(values: list[int]) -> int:
    """Count index triples whose values sum to zero."""
    n = len(values)
    count = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            for k in range(j + 1, n):
                if values[i] + values[j] + values[k] == 0:
                    count += 1
    return count

Before timing it: which test would persuade you that it counts the intended triples?

21:00–24:00. Walk through why the increasing indices avoid permutations and reusing one element. Ask for a small hand-worked test. Correctness checks should be shared by every later implementation.

What does input size mean here?

Let (n) be the number of integers.

The running time is a function (T(n)), but it can also depend on:

  • the actual values in the input;
  • the Python implementation and libraries;
  • the processor, memory and cache;
  • the operating system and other work on the machine.

So how can we measure it sensibly?

24:00–26:00. Define n explicitly. Avoid saying that the algorithm alone always determines the exponent and the input only determines a coefficient; some algorithms have input-dependent best, average and worst cases.

Measure before you model

from statistics import median
from time import perf_counter

def elapsed_seconds(function, argument, repetitions=5):
    function(argument)  # untimed warm-up
    times = []
    for _ in range(repetitions):
        start = perf_counter()
        function(argument)
        times.append(perf_counter() - start)
    return median(times)
  • Use several input sizes.
  • Repeat timings and report the median.
  • Time equivalent work and record the environment.
  • Check the result as well as the clock.

26:00–29:30. This strengthens the source deck’s single-run perf_counter example. perf_counter is appropriate for elapsed-duration measurements. A warm-up and median do not remove all noise, but they are a defensible classroom baseline. Do not include file reading or printing when comparing only the algorithm.

What pattern do the measurements suggest?

If multiplying (n) by 2 multiplies time by about 8, that is evidence consistent with cubic growth because (2^3 = 8).

29:30–32:00. Ask students to predict the multiplier before revealing it. The plot is historical evidence from the source lecture, not a benchmark for their machine. A log-log line can suggest a power law; it does not prove one.

A useful empirical model

Suppose the measurements are consistent with

[ T(n) a n^b. ]

Taking logarithms gives

[ T(n) a + bn. ]

The slope (b) describes the observed scaling over the measured range. The coefficient (a) absorbs machine- and implementation-dependent costs.

32:00–35:00. This makes explicit the log transformation behind the original regression slide. State the limitation: a fitted power law is an empirical model over the tested sizes. Small inputs, cache boundaries or mixed operations can produce a different pattern.

Faster hardware changes the coefficient—not the question

A faster computer may reduce every measured time. It does not usually change the number of triples examined by this algorithm.

How long until growth in the input consumes the hardware gain?

35:00–37:30. The exact hardware comparison in the original figure is a period illustration, not a current benchmark. The conceptual point remains useful: constant-factor improvements cannot indefinitely compensate for a poor growth rate.

From timings to a mathematical model

In principle, running time is a sum of

[ . ]

Exact costs are awkward and machine-dependent. Instead:

  1. choose an operation that captures the main repeated work; and
  2. count how often the algorithm performs it as (n) grows.

37:30–40:00. Do not use the source deck’s old nanosecond table as if it were a current universal measurement. Assignment, arithmetic, indexing and function calls have different costs, and Python objects add overhead. We want a useful model, not false precision.

A simple cost model: 1-SUM

def count_zeros(values: list[int]) -> int:
    count = 0
    for value in values:
        if value == 0:
            count += 1
    return count

If comparison with zero is the chosen operation, how many comparisons occur for a list of length (n)?

Exactly (n)—whether the list contains no zeroes or many.

40:00–43:00. The source calls this 1-SUM. Use a descriptive function name while retaining the example. Students should identify the comparison as the counted operation. Other operations matter to elapsed time, but they also grow linearly.

Keep the part that governs growth

Suppose an operation count is

[ 4n^3 + 2n^2 + 16. ]

For large (n), the (n^3) term dominates. We therefore describe the growth as

[ (n^3). ]

This discards the leading coefficient and lower-order terms—not because they never matter, but because the model is asking how the work scales.

43:00–46:00. Correct the original line that said small n does not matter. Constants and lower-order terms can decide which implementation is faster for the input sizes we actually use. Asymptotic notation addresses the large-input trend.

Big Theta and Big O are not interchangeable

  • (Theta(g(n))): a tight asymptotic growth class—both an upper and lower bound.
  • (O(g(n))): an asymptotic upper bound.

If an algorithm takes (Theta(n)) work, it is also (O(n^2)), but (O(n^2)) does not describe it tightly.

In informal conversation people often say “Big O” when they mean order of growth. Here we will use (Theta) when claiming a tight class.

46:00–49:00. This resolves the source deck’s mixture of Big Theta and Big O. Do not turn the session into a proof course. Students need to interpret and compare growth classes accurately.

Common orders of growth

49:00–52:30. Read the plot from left to right. Linear and n log n algorithms often remain useful at much larger n than quadratic or cubic ones. That is a guide, not a universal runtime ranking: coefficients, libraries and input size still matter.

What happens when the input doubles?

Growth Approximate multiplier when (n2n)
(1) 1
(log n) slightly more than 1
(n) 2
(nn) a little more than 2
(n^2) 4
(n^3) 8
(2^n) squares its previous value

Predict first: which pattern should the triple loop show?

52:30–55:30. This is a practical way to connect experiments with asymptotic classes. Doubling ratios are approximate when lower-order terms and overheads are visible.

Break

When we return: can a different data structure turn a quadratic algorithm into a linear one?

55:30–65:30. Ten-minute break.

Worked comparison: 2-SUM

Given a collection of distinct integers, count the pairs whose sum is zero.

Before seeing code:

  • What result do you expect for [3, -3, 5, 8, -8]?
  • What should happen for an empty list?
  • Why does “distinct integers” matter?

65:30–67:30. Expected answer is two pairs. Ask students to state whether pairs refer to values or indices. The distinct-value assumption lets the simple set algorithm below count each complementary pair once.

Approach 1: compare every pair

def count_two_sum_brute(values: list[int]) -> int:
    count = 0
    n = len(values)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if values[i] + values[j] == 0:
                count += 1
    return count

The number of comparisons is

[ , ]

so the running time is (Theta(n^2)).

67:30–70:30. Ask why j begins at i+1. Expand n(n-1)/2 only as far as needed to see the n-squared leading term.

Approach 2: remember what we have seen

def count_two_sum_set(values: list[int]) -> int:
    seen: set[int] = set()
    count = 0
    for value in values:
        if -value in seen:
            count += 1
        seen.add(value)
    return count

With average constant-time set lookup and insertion:

  • expected running time: (Theta(n));
  • additional memory: (Theta(n)).

70:30–74:00. Trace one pair. Make the assumption explicit: Python set lookup is average constant time, not an unconditional worst-case guarantee. This approach trades memory for speed.

Same answer? Check before celebrating

examples = [
    ([], 0),
    ([4], 0),
    ([3, -3, 5, 8, -8], 2),
    ([-10, -2, 0, 6, 10], 1),
]

for values, expected in examples:
    assert count_two_sum_brute(values) == expected
    assert count_two_sum_set(values) == expected

These checks support the stated distinct-integer problem. They do not show that the set version counts every index pair correctly when values repeat.

74:00–77:00. This limitation is deliberate. For example, repeated zeroes or multiple copies of a complementary value require a frequency-aware algorithm if the task is to count index pairs. Performance comparisons are meaningless when the implementations solve different problems.

Practical: predict, test and explain scaling

In pairs:

  1. Copy the two 2-SUM functions into a fresh script.
  2. Add the shared correctness checks.
  3. Predict the growth class of each implementation and the effect of doubling (n).
  4. Generate distinct inputs of several sizes with known or independently checked answers.
  5. After one warm-up, record the median of at least five timings for each size.
  6. Decide whether the evidence agrees with your prediction.

Record the environment and time only the pair-counting function—not input generation, printing or plotting.

77:00–92:00. Give students fifteen minutes. Provide a prepared timing table if machines or setup fail. Discourage very large brute-force inputs. The goal is to connect a prediction to evidence, not to freeze the room for the longest run.

Practical debrief

Be ready to explain:

  • whether both functions passed the same checks;
  • how elapsed time changed when (n) doubled;
  • why the set changes the amount of repeated work;
  • what extra memory the faster algorithm uses; and
  • one limitation of your measurement.

92:00–97:00. Invite two comparisons, preferably including one noisy result. Treat disagreement as a reason to inspect input sizes, repetitions and timed work rather than as failure.

Memory is part of performance

Ask how the largest amount of memory held at one time grows with (n).

  • The brute-force 2-SUM loop uses little additional memory: (Theta(1)).
  • The set-based algorithm stores up to (n) values: (Theta(n)).

The faster algorithm is not free. It exchanges memory for fewer comparisons.

97:00–100:00. This develops the source deck’s brief memory slide into an explicit time-memory trade-off. Distinguish additional working memory from the memory already occupied by the input.

Improve the algorithm before buying hardware

A change from (Theta(n^2)) to expected (Theta(n)) can save orders of magnitude. Adding processors usually changes performance by a bounded factor.

100:00–102:30. Use the original table qualitatively; its exact solvable sizes depend on operation cost and hardware. The ordering is the lesson.

Parallelism and HPC: the next layer

Parallelism performs independent operations at the same time.

High-performance computing (HPC) provides larger or specialised resources—such as many CPU cores, GPUs or high-memory nodes—for suitable workloads.

  • Independent simulations or parameter combinations may parallelise well.
  • Steps that depend on previous results remain sequential.
  • Coordination and data movement also cost time.

Choose a suitable algorithm first; then ask whether parallel hardware helps.

102:30–105:30. Keep this conceptual. Operational HPC teaching is outside this session and remains under separate MQB review. Avoid implying that moving code to a cluster automatically makes it faster.

What should you now be able to do?

Given two implementations of the same problem, you should be able to:

  1. state the input, output and assumptions;
  2. check that both produce the intended result;
  3. measure comparable runs over several input sizes;
  4. predict and explain their orders of growth;
  5. identify a time-memory trade-off; and
  6. justify which implementation you would use.

105:30–108:00. Return to the opening question. The answer is not simply “use the fastest”. It depends on correctness, expected input sizes, memory, clarity and how often the work will be repeated.

Next: notebooks and evidence

On Thursday, use a clean notebook to present:

  • the problem and assumptions;
  • the shared correctness checks;
  • the timing method and results;
  • the predicted and observed scaling; and
  • your reason for accepting or rejecting any suggested improvement.

The notebook explains the evidence. The reusable functions still belong in a script that can be tested independently.

108:00–110:00. This is the handoff to Thursday’s scheduled notebook work. If an AI tool proposes a change, students must test it against the independent baseline established before assistance.
